claims.claim: A Wizards of the Coast adventure designer states on the publisher's own site that boxed text is named for the line that marks it to be read aloud.
claims.source: Shawn Merwin, 'Let's Design an Adventure: Boxed Text', D&D Beyond, 6 Nov 2019
claims.quote: denoting that it should be read aloud to the players

claims.claim: The same designer's first tip is to write boxed text in the third person rather than the second.
claims.source: Shawn Merwin, 'Let's Design an Adventure: Boxed Text', D&D Beyond, 6 Nov 2019
claims.quote: Move from the second-person point of view to the third person

claims.claim: He gives as the reason that dropping the second person makes it hard to attribute actions or feelings to the characters.
claims.source: Shawn Merwin, 'Let's Design an Adventure: Boxed Text', D&D Beyond, 6 Nov 2019
claims.quote: it’s difficult to inadvertently include character actions, motivations, feelings, or movements

claims.claim: The same designer rules the novelist's impulse out of boxed text.
claims.source: Shawn Merwin, 'Let's Design an Adventure: Boxed Text', D&D Beyond, 6 Nov 2019
claims.quote: boxed text is not the place to unleash that inner novelist

claims.claim: He rules that boxed text must describe only what the characters can sense.
claims.source: Shawn Merwin, 'Let's Design an Adventure: Boxed Text', D&D Beyond, 6 Nov 2019
claims.quote: Describe everything the characters can sense, but not what they can’t

claims.claim: He measures his own model boxed text at four sentences and under a hundred words.
claims.source: Shawn Merwin, 'Let's Design an Adventure: Boxed Text', D&D Beyond, 6 Nov 2019
claims.quote: Four sentences, and less than 100 words.

claims.claim: He assigns the opening sentence of a scene the job of setting tone and introducing the scene.
claims.source: Shawn Merwin, 'Let's Design an Adventure: Boxed Text', D&D Beyond, 6 Nov 2019
claims.quote: The first sentence sets the tone and introduces the scene

claims.claim: The 2024 free rules define boxed text as text meant to be read aloud when the characters first arrive at a location.
claims.source: Wizards of the Coast, D&D Free Rules (2024), 'The Basics'
claims.quote: meant to be read aloud to the players when their characters

claims.claim: The same 2024 free-rules paragraph says boxed text usually describes locations.
claims.source: Wizards of the Coast, D&D Free Rules (2024), 'The Basics'
claims.quote: It usually describes locations so the players know what’s happening

claims.claim: The publisher's own 2024 rules put the attention limit for descriptive text at about three sentences.
claims.source: Wizards of the Coast, D&D Free Rules (2024), 'The Basics'
claims.quote: lose focus after about three sentences of descriptive text

claims.claim: The D&D story lead states in his own collected columns that he keeps his descriptions spare.
claims.source: Christopher Perkins, The Dungeon Master Experience 2011 collected columns, Wizards of the Coast

claims.claim: The same designer says he does not frontload information.
claims.source: Christopher Perkins, The Dungeon Master Experience 2011 collected columns, Wizards of the Coast

claims.claim: The same designer says he builds his human surnames on roots from western European cultures.
claims.source: Christopher Perkins, 'The Dungeon Master Experience: What's in a Name?', collected 2011 columns, Wizards of the Coast
claims.quote: and last names with roots in western European cultures

claims.claim: A settlement-generator vendor attributes a population tier set of hamlet 50-300, village 300-900 and town 1,000-8,000 to the Dungeon Master's Guide, figures that match neither the publisher's own 2024 settlement handout nor any edition it names.
claims.source: Vito, 'D&D Settlement Sizes — Hamlet, Village, Town, and City', Tools and Taverns, updated 13 Jul 2026
claims.quote: DMG population tiers: hamlet 50-300, village 300-900, town 1,000-8,000

verdicts.trueWording: denoting that it should be read aloud to the players
verdicts.note: Raw HTML fetched (200, 319KB). Opening paragraph: boxed text 'got its name from the thin boxed-line that sometimes surrounds the text', with the quoted clause following word for word. Byline 'by Shawn Merwin'; his bio lists WotC-published credits (Acquisitions Incorporated, Baldur's Gate: Descent into Avernus, Storm Lord's Wrath) and an Adventurers League role, so 'a Wizards of the Coast adventure designer' is supported as a designer of WotC adventures, not as a stated employee. Site footer carries 'Wizards of the Coast LLC | All Rights Reserved'. FLAG (external, not verified from the page): the article is dated Nov 2019, when D&D Beyond was operated by Fandom/Curse; WotC ownership came later, so 'the publisher's own site' holds for the page as fetched today, not necessarily at publication.

verdicts.trueWording: Move from the second-person point of view to the third person
verdicts.note: Exact heading of 'Tip 1', the first of six numbered tips. Claim limb 'first tip' confirmed: the tip list begins at Tip 1 immediately after the worked bad example.

verdicts.trueWording: difficult to inadvertently include character actions, motivations, feelings, or movements
verdicts.note: Body of 'Tip 1', word for word including the curly apostrophe in 'it's'. The full sentence supplies the causal limb: 'If we do not use the word “you” as the subject of the sentences in boxed text, it's difficult...' — so the reason limb ('dropping the second person makes it hard to attribute actions or feelings') is supported.

verdicts.trueWording: boxed text is not the place to unleash that inner novelist
verdicts.note: Body of 'Tip 2. Avoid the novelist/dramatist urge', word for word. The section then enumerates three sub-problems (2a purple detail, 2b villain soliloquy, 2c action in progress), which supports 'rules the novelist's impulse out'.

verdicts.trueWording: Describe everything the characters can sense, but not what they can't
verdicts.note: Exact heading of 'Tip 3' (curly apostrophe in 'can't'). Body confirms both halves: text must not omit the obvious (the 50-foot chasm) and must not detail what characters could not know (crates' contents).

verdicts.trueWording: Four sentences, and less than 100 words.
verdicts.note: Exact sentence opening the analysis under 'A Boxed-Text Opening', immediately after his own carrion-crows sample. It is his measurement of his own model text, as the claim states.

verdicts.trueWording: The first sentence sets the tone and introduces the scene
verdicts.note: Word for word under 'A Boxed-Text Opening'; the page continues 'using words like “carrion” and “bloody.”' He then assigns jobs to sentences two, three and four in the same paragraph, so the sentence-role framing is the section's own.

verdicts.trueWording: meant to be read aloud to the players when their characters
verdicts.note: Raw HTML fetched (200, 246KB). Third paragraph under 'Step 1: Describe the Situation': 'Published adventures often include text in a box like this, which is meant to be read aloud to the players when their characters first arrive at a location or under a specific circumstance.' Two scope notes: the page never uses the phrase 'boxed text' (it says 'text in a box like this'), and it adds a second trigger, 'or under a specific circumstance', which the claim omits without denying. Source-name note: the page and its breadcrumb label this 'Basic Rules', not 'Free Rules'; the URL path is br-2024 and it is the 2024 line (a separate 'Basic Rules (2014)' is linked), so the '2024' limb is confirmed.

verdicts.trueWording: It usually describes locations so the players know what's happening
verdicts.note: Same paragraph as index 1205, sentence two, word for word; the paragraph continues 'and have a sense of what their characters' options are'. The 'same paragraph' limb is confirmed — both quotes sit in one paragraph under 'Step 1: Describe the Situation'.

verdicts.trueWording: lose focus after about three sentences of descriptive text
verdicts.note: Word for word in the paragraph directly after the boxed-text paragraph, still under 'Step 1: Describe the Situation': 'Most players begin to lose focus after about three sentences of descriptive text.' Scope note: the rules say players 'begin to lose focus after about' three sentences — a hedged observation rather than a prescribed cap; the claim's word 'limit' is firmer than the page, though the quoted hedge travels with it. Publisher limb supported by the WotC LLC footer on the fetched page.

verdicts.unsupportedLimb: 'The D&D story lead' — the source names Perkins D&D Senior Producer, not story lead
verdicts.note: Wayback raw PDF fetched (200, 3.8MB, PDF 1.7) and text-extracted with pdftotext. The quoted sentence appears word for word in the December 2011 / Dungeon 197 installment, whose running head is 'The Dungeon Master Experience: T'wit' — the pacing column on 'the ancient art of contraction', not a column titled 'Pacing' as the claim's page field says. It heads one of his listed tactics: 'I keep my descriptions spare. If the characters are hired to escort a merchant caravan...' The collected-columns limb is supported (the PDF is the compiled 2011 DM Experience columns). The unsupported limb is the title: the PDF's author blocks read 'Chris Perkins is the D&D Senior Producer at Wizards of the Coast LLC' and 'he's the senior producer for the Dungeons & Dragons Roleplaying Game and leads the team of designers, developers, and editors' — nothing in the source calls him a story lead.

Word for word (curly apostrophe) in the same December 2011 / Dungeon 197 pacing column, a few tactics below index 1208's sentence: 'I don't frontload information. I let it trickle out in dribs and drabs...' The claim sentence carries no job-title limb (it says only 'the same designer'), so it verifies where 1208 goes PARTIAL.

verdicts.trueWording: and last names with roots in western European cultures
verdicts.note: Found in 'The Dungeon Master Experience: What's in a Name?' in the same collected PDF. The only break is the PDF's typographic line-break hyphen ('cul-tures'); reading order confirms the words are contiguous. Full sentence: 'I tend to go for names that sound like seldom used real-world names (e.g., Arando, Caven, Fenton, Mirabel, Remora) and last names with roots in western European cultures (e.g., Caskajaro, Moonridge, Ratley, Van Hyden), or names built around nautical terms.' Scope note: he prefaces it with 'My human names are all over the map' and offers nautical-term names as an alternative, so this is a stated tendency among several, not his only surname rule — the claim's 'says he builds' does not overreach that, but a downstream use should not read it as an exclusive rule.

verdicts.unsupportedLimb: that the figures match no WotC edition nor the 2024 settlement handout — the page makes no comparison and names no edition
verdicts.trueWording: DMG population tiers: hamlet 50-300, village 300-900, town 1,000-8,000
verdicts.note: Raw HTML fetched (200, 25KB). The quote is the exact opening of the first 'Key Takeaways' bullet, which continues ', city 8,000+, metropolis 25,000+.' The vendor limb is supported: the site sells/hosts a 'D&D Settlement Generator' it links from this guide. The attribution limb is supported twice — the bullet's 'DMG population tiers' and the body's 'The Dungeon Master's Guide splits settlements into rough tiers by population'. What this page cannot support is the claim's second half: it names no edition of the DMG and makes no comparison to any WotC handout, so the mismatch assertion needs a separate source and is not verified here.
